### Reference Status

This is the single-file full reference manuscript for the tangent-space material.
It is retained for derivations, appendices, and historical traceability. The
canonical rendered reading path is the compact seven-part
[Tangent-Space Series](../tangent-hyperplanes-series/part-1-geometry.html), which

:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
### Thesis Abstract

A golf swing couples changing posture, segment momentum, shaft deformation, applied torque and contact. Several useful linear relations survive inside this nonlinear motion, but they answer different questions. A differentiable model has a linear derivative at a specified state and input. A control-affine model additionally has an exact finite input-to-rate increment relation at a fixed state. The first variation of a trajectory satisfies a linear differential equation along a common reference motion. None of these facts makes independently evolving swings additive.

Part I develops these distinctions, their geometric meaning, and the regularity needed for error bounds. Part II derives how an entire input perturbation is transported into an endpoint change and how an adjoint weights it by a chosen outcome. Part III develops optimal-control methods subject to their own assumptions. The purpose is a technically usable account of local modeling, with explicit limits on finite predictions and physical interpretation.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
### A Note on "Exactness"

The derivative and first-variation equation are exact mathematical objects. Replacing a finite nonlinear response by its first-order expansion is an approximation. Continuous differentiability gives a little-o remainder; a quadratic bound needs additional regularity. Exact fixed-state force addition is a separate mechanical statement about a specified input map. Keep these meanings distinct throughout the [canonical rendered reading path](../tangent-hyperplanes-series/part-1-geometry.html).
:::

## Part I: Geometric Foundations and Local Dynamics {.unnumbered}

## Introduction and Motivation

### The Central Thesis

Suppose a model predicts the body's and club's future state from initial conditions and an applied-torque history. Three experiments ask three different questions:

1. At the same posture, velocity and shaft state, how does an extra torque change acceleration now?
2. Along a specified reference swing, how does a small perturbation change the eventual clubhead state to first order?
3. If that torque history is actually changed by a finite amount, what new motion and impact follow?

The first can have an exact affine answer. The second is a derivative of the model's solution map. The third generally requires a new nonlinear integration, including any changed event time. Their relationship explains the usefulness of linear methods without extending their conclusions beyond their hypotheses.

### Central Claim

For a differentiable coordinate model, the map from state/input perturbation directions to the **first variation of state rate** is linear. If the model is also affine in the declared input, finite input increments produce exactly linear rate increments while state, time and mode remain fixed. Along a common reference, first variations propagate linearly. These are properties of the model and its derivatives; they do not establish biological intent, individual muscle recruitment or optimal swing technique.

### Scope: No Trajectory Superposition

For a homogeneous linear system, linear combinations of solutions are solutions. For a linear system with a fixed nonzero forcing, differences about a common particular solution obey the homogeneous equation. Even in the linear case, adding two complete forced solutions would double the common forcing.

For a nonlinear system, the finite input-to-trajectory map generally fails to be additive. This can happen on ordinary Euclidean space with its usual flat geometry. Curvature of the state manifold is neither required nor a universal measure of the error.

### Terminology: "Tangent Hyperplane" as Affine Subspace

At fixed state $x$, a control-affine model has rates $f_0(x)+G(x)u$. For unrestricted $u\in\mathbb R^m$, this image is the affine subspace $f_0(x)+\operatorname{im}G(x)$ of $T_x\mathcal M$. It is a hyperplane only when its codimension is one. With bounded admissible inputs $\mathcal U(x)$, the actual instantaneous rate set is $f_0(x)+G(x)\mathcal U(x)$, usually only part of that subspace. This set is not the finite-time reachable set.

### Scope and Prerequisites

We use a finite-dimensional state chart and one smooth contact/constraint mode. Assume a unique reference solution exists on the stated finite interval, and all compared solutions remain in the model domain. For the initial derivations, take $f$ continuous in time and continuously differentiable in state and input on a neighborhood of those solutions. Piecewise continuous prescribed inputs can be handled on each smooth time segment. More general measurable inputs require corresponding uniform regularity and integrability hypotheses.

State and input components should have declared units or nondimensional scales before norms are compared. A configuration $q$ is not the complete dynamic state: velocity, shaft modes and retained actuator states matter. At impacts, saturation switches, friction transitions or changing constraint rank, ordinary smooth derivatives may cease to describe the experiment. A smooth equality-constrained system can be reduced to a regular chart; an active inequality or contact transition needs additional analysis.

## Tangent Spaces and Exact Differentiation

### Nonlinear Dynamics and Smoothness

In local coordinates, let

$$
\dot x=f(x,u,t),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^n,\quad u\in\mathbb R^m.
$$ {#eq-thesis-dynamics}

Fix $(\bar x,\bar u,t)$ and combine the perturbations into $h=(h_x,h_u)$. Fréchet differentiability means there is a linear map $D f$ such that

$$
f(\bar x+h_x,\bar u+h_u,t)
=f(\bar x,\bar u,t)+D f(\bar x,\bar u,t)[h]+r(h),
$$ {#eq-frechet}

$$
\lim_{\|h\|\to0}\frac{\|r(h)\|}{\|h\|}=0.
$$ {#eq-little-o}

The limit controls arbitrary directions approaching zero in the chosen norm. It does not say $r(h)=0$ at a nonzero perturbation. Differentiability at a point does not require a continuous derivative in a whole neighborhood; $C^1$ is a useful stronger hypothesis that gives uniform control on compact neighborhoods and supports the flow results used here.

### Continuous Differentiability Does Not Give a Quadratic Bound

The scalar function $F(z)=|z|^{3/2}$ is $C^1$ near zero and $F'(0)=0$. Its remainder is $|h|^{3/2}$. Dividing by $|h|$ gives a quantity tending to zero, as required for differentiability. Dividing by $h^2$ gives $|h|^{-1/2}$, which is unbounded. Thus a blanket $O(\|h\|^2)$ claim under only $C^1$ assumptions is false.

A locally Lipschitz derivative, often denoted $C^{1,1}$, is sufficient for a quadratic bound. If $\|Df(z+s h)-Df(z)\|\leq L_D s\|h\|$ along the segment, then

$$
r(h)=\int_0^1\bigl(Df(z+s h)-Df(z)\bigr)h\,ds,
\qquad \|r(h)\|\leq\tfrac12 L_D\|h\|^2.
$$

A continuous bounded second derivative on the relevant neighborhood also supplies this bound. The neighborhood, norm, constant and permissible amplitudes are part of the statement, not optional details.

### Directional Derivatives

For a Fréchet-differentiable map, each directional derivative agrees with the same linear map:

$$
\left.\frac{d}{d\epsilon}f(z+\epsilon h,t)\right|_{\epsilon=0}
=Df(z,t)[h].
$$ {#eq-directional}

Existence of derivatives along every line does not by itself establish this property. Define $F(a,b)=a^3/(a^2+b^2)$ away from the origin and $F(0,0)=0$. It is continuous at the origin, and its derivative along direction $(a,b)$ is $a^3/(a^2+b^2)$. The directions $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ give 1 and 0, while their sum gives $1/2$. These directional derivatives do not constitute a linear derivative.

### The Jacobian Matrices

Under differentiability, the coordinate derivative has blocks

$$
A(t)=f_x(\bar x(t),\bar u(t),t),\qquad
A_{ij}=\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j},
$$ {#eq-jacobian-A}

$$
B(t)=f_u(\bar x(t),\bar u(t),t),\qquad
B_{ij}=\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial u_j}.
$$ {#eq-jacobian-B}

The exact first variation of the rate is $A h_x+B h_u$. Both matrices use the same reference state, input and time. A derivative evaluated on one counterfactual branch cannot silently be substituted for that of another.

### A Tangent Space Is Not a Derivative

The tangent space $T_x\mathcal M$ is the vector space of velocities of curves through $x$ on a smooth manifold. It exists independently of any particular dynamic law. A smooth map $F:\mathcal M\to\mathcal N$ has a derivative $T_xF:T_x\mathcal M\to T_{F(x)}\mathcal N$. The space and the map are different objects.

A vector field assigns $f(x)\in T_x\mathcal M$. Geometrically it is a section $\mathcal M\to T\mathcal M$; its derivative therefore maps into the tangent space of the **tangent bundle**, not automatically back into $T_x\mathcal M$. Local coordinates or an explicitly chosen connection give the familiar component formulas. A state-rate Jacobian along a moving reference is a valid coordinate representation of the variational dynamics; it is not an intrinsic endomorphism independent of that choice.

For a family of solutions $x_\epsilon(t)$ with prescribed $u_\epsilon=\bar u+\epsilon v$ and $x_\epsilon(t_0)=\bar x_0+\epsilon\eta_0$, define

$$
\eta(t)=\left.\frac{\partial x_\epsilon(t)}{\partial\epsilon}\right|_0,
\qquad \dot\eta=A(t)\eta+B(t)v(t),\quad\eta(t_0)=\eta_0.
$$ {#eq-tangent-dynamics}

This equation follows by differentiating the dynamic equation with respect to the family parameter. $\eta$ is a derivative with respect to amplitude, not the full finite displacement $x_\epsilon-\bar x$. Under the stated regularity on a fixed common interval, the latter is $\epsilon\eta+o(\epsilon)$.

### Coordinate Changes Along a Moving Motion

For a smooth invertible coordinate change $y=\psi(x)$, write $T(t)=D\psi(\bar x(t))$. Variations satisfy $\eta_y=T\eta_x$. Differentiating this identity gives

$$
A_y=(\dot T+T A_x)T^{-1},\qquad B_y=T B_x.
$$

The additional $\dot T$ term is essential away from an equilibrium. For $\dot x=1$ on $x>0$ and $y=x^2$, $A_x=0$, while $\dot y=2\sqrt y$ has $A_y=1/x$. A constant $\eta_x$ corresponds to $\eta_y=2x\eta_x$, which grows as $x$ grows. This is the same physical separation represented in different units and coordinates. At an equilibrium of an autonomous system, $\dot T=0$ and the Jacobians are similar, so their eigenvalues agree.

This matters when comparing a joint-space perturbation with a clubhead-space perturbation. A growing coordinate norm need not mean that the physically chosen task error grows at the same rate.

### Example: The Simple Pendulum

For a point mass $m$ at length $\ell$, torque $u$, and angle $\theta$ measured from downward vertical,

$$
m\ell^2\ddot\theta+mg\ell\sin\theta=u.
$$ {#eq-pendulum-second-order}

With $x=(\theta,\omega)$,

$$
f(x,u)=\begin{pmatrix}\omega\\-(g/\ell)\sin\theta+u/(m\ell^2)\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-pendulum-state-space}

The derivative is

$$
D f[h_x,h_u]=A h_x+B h_u,
$$ {#eq-pendulum-jacobian-def}

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-(g/\ell)\cos\bar\theta&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1/(m\ell^2)\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-pendulum-jacobian}

Along any reference solution,

$$
\dot\eta_\theta=\eta_\omega,\qquad
\dot\eta_\omega=-(g/\ell)\cos\bar\theta(t)\eta_\theta
+v/(m\ell^2).
$$ {#eq-pendulum-linearized}

At the unforced downward equilibrium, this becomes

$$
\ddot\eta_\theta+(g/\ell)\eta_\theta=0,
$$ {#eq-pendulum-harmonic}

$$
\lambda_{1,2}=\pm i\sqrt{g/\ell}.
$$ {#eq-pendulum-eigenvalues}

Pure imaginary eigenvalues do not prove stability of the nonlinear equilibrium by the indirect method. Here a separate energy argument does: $E=\tfrac12m\ell^2\omega^2+mg\ell(1-\cos\theta)$ is conserved and has a strict local minimum at $(0,0)$. Sufficiently small sublevel sets remain in a small neighborhood. The equilibrium is locally Lyapunov stable, but nearby positive-energy motions cannot converge to it without dissipation.

For comparison, the planar systems $\dot z=Jz\pm\|z\|^2z$, with $J$ a unit rotation generator, have the same imaginary eigenvalues at the origin. Their radii satisfy $\dot r=\pm r^3$: one decays and the other grows. The derivative alone leaves that distinction unresolved.

The pendulum's finite-angle discrepancy can be seen from

$$
\sin\theta=\theta-\theta^3/6+O(\theta^5).
$$ {#eq-sin-taylor}

At this particular equilibrium the first omitted state term is cubic by symmetry. Generic nonlinear models need not have that cancellation.

### Exact Superposition of Input Increments

Linearity of $Df$ gives additivity of derivative directions for any differentiable model. Exact finite input additivity needs the stronger structural condition

$$
f(x,u,t)=f_0(x,t)+G(x,t)u.
$$

At fixed $(x,t)$, with one nominal input $\bar u$, define $\Delta_i=f(x,\bar u+v_i,t)-f(x,\bar u,t)$. Then the combined increment is exactly $\Delta_{12}=G(v_1+v_2)=\Delta_1+\Delta_2$. The baseline rate appears once. This statement can hold for finite increments without making the state dependence linear.

For regular mechanical coordinates, $M(q)\ddot q+h(q,\dot q,t)=\mathcal B(q)u$ has this property when $M$ is nonsingular and neither $M$ nor $h$ depends on the declared input. Applied forces are covectors; $M^{-1}\mathcal B$ maps them into acceleration increments. Equality-constraint reactions can preserve affinity after a regular linear solve. A fixed contact mode alone does not guarantee it: a nonlinear actuator law, such as torque proportional to the square of a command, must be inspected in the actual command variable.

If the input set has bounds, the algebraic identity applies whenever the compared inputs are defined; all inputs must also be admissible for a feasible experiment. Bounds do not turn an arbitrary nonlinear actuator into a piecewise linear one.

### Counterfactual Decomposition

Where the zero-input branch is defined,

$$
f(x,u,t)=f(x,0,t)+G(x,t)u.
$$ {#eq-counterfactual}

This is a decomposition evaluated at **one state**. Along an actual motion, integrating the two vector-valued terms in a common coordinate chart reconstructs that motion's coordinate increment. The integral of $f(x(t),0,t)$ generally does not equal a forward zero-input motion, which evaluates $f$ at its own evolving state. A coordinate increment, a scalar speed, work and a changed impact outcome are different quantities.

## Time Evolution and Moving Tangent Spaces

### Why Global Superposition Fails

Along a reference motion the coefficients are

$$
A(t)=f_x(\bar x(t),\bar u(t),t),\qquad
B(t)=f_u(\bar x(t),\bar u(t),t).
$$ {#eq-time-varying-jacobians}

Changing the finite input generally changes the entire state history and hence these coefficients. Integrating a derivative on the old history predicts the first variation of the new history, not its complete finite change.

### Flow Transport Is Not Parallel Transport

On $\mathbb R^n$, tangent vectors at different points have a canonical identification as ordinary vectors. Adding them is mathematically meaningful. Nevertheless, for $\dot x=x^2$ on the flat real line,

$$
\varphi_T(x_0)=\frac{x_0}{1-Tx_0},\qquad
D\varphi_T(x_0)=\frac{1}{(1-Tx_0)^2},
$$

on an interval before the denominator vanishes. The flow is nonlinear although the space has zero intrinsic curvature. Its derivative transports a perturbation according to the dynamic law. Euclidean parallel transport instead leaves vector components constant; it is a different operation.

More generally, $T\varphi_{t,s}$ transports initial tangent perturbations to the current state along a fixed prescribed input history. It does not require introducing a metric connection. If a connection is used to compare vectors or define norms, state the choice and do not equate its parallel transport with the dynamic solution derivative.

### Separate the Two Refinement Experiments

For sufficiently smooth time dependence, the full nonlinear solution has

$$
\begin{aligned}
x(t+h)&=x(t)+h f(t)\\
&\quad+\tfrac12h^2\bigl(f_x f+f_u\dot u+f_t\bigr)+O(h^3).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-taylor-time}

Here $f(t)=f(x(t),u(t),t)$. A bounded third time derivative is a sufficient condition for the displayed remainder. $C^1$ state dependence and arbitrary input histories do not provide it. At an input jump, integrate on each time segment with the appropriate one-sided behavior.

Euler's method recomputes the **full nonlinear** rate at its numerical state. Under suitable regularity, consistency and stability on a common finite interval, reducing its step size $h$ converges to the nonlinear solution. Integrating the first-variation equation with smaller $h$ instead converges to the first variation.

For the exact scalar flow above, the error of predicting a finite initial increment $\epsilon$ by $\varphi_T(x_0)+\epsilon D\varphi_T(x_0)$ is

$$
\frac{T\epsilon^2}
{(1-Tx_0)^2(1-Tx_0-T\epsilon)}.
$$ {#eq-limit-exactness}

With $x_0=1$, $T=0.2$ and $\epsilon=0.1$ in nondimensional variables, the error is about $0.00400641$, even with exact integration. It disappears as amplitude tends to zero, not as a solver step tends to zero at fixed amplitude.

### Variational Equation

The precise local statement is therefore

$$
\dot\eta=A(t)\eta+B(t)v(t),\qquad
x_\epsilon(t)=\bar x(t)+\epsilon\eta(t)+o(\epsilon),
$$ {#eq-variational}

uniformly on a suitable fixed finite interval. A stronger quadratic remainder requires correspondingly stronger regularity and neighborhood bounds. Verify integration convergence and perturbation-amplitude convergence separately. This is the bridge from exact differentiation to a defensible finite prediction.

The standard flow and equilibrium results are discussed in [Hunter's ODE notes, Sections 1.3–1.4](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/m207/m207.pdf). The distinction between directional and norm-controlled functional variation is developed in [Liberzon, Section 1.3.2](https://liberzon.csl.illinois.edu/teaching/cvoc.pdf). The counterexamples above make the specific limitations used here explicit.

## Local Optimal Control: LQR and Lyapunov Stability

### Connection to Linear Quadratic Regulation

A local derivative model supports controller design when paired with a stated objective and a separate stability argument.

#### The LQR Problem

Linear Quadratic Regulation (LQR) solves the following problem:

**Given:**

- Linear system: $\dot{x} = Ax + Bu$
- Quadratic cost: $J = \int_0^\infty (x^T Q x + u^T R u) dt$
- Matrices $Q \succeq 0$ (positive semidefinite), $R \succ 0$ (positive definite)

**Find:** Optimal feedback control law minimizing $J$

**Solution:** Linear state feedback $u = -Kx$ where gain $K$ is computed by solving the **algebraic Riccati equation**:

$$
A^T P + P A - P B R^{-1} B^T P + Q = 0
$$ {#eq-riccati}

with $K = R^{-1} B^T P$. Standard sufficient assumptions for the stabilizing infinite-horizon solution are stabilizability of $(A,B)$ and detectability of $(Q^{1/2},A)$. Select the stabilizing positive-semidefinite solution; the matrix equation alone does not guarantee that an arbitrary root defines an optimal stabilizer.

#### What a Nonlinear LQR Design Establishes

At an equilibrium, a differentiable nonlinear system has a linear first variation. If the resulting closed-loop Jacobian is Hurwitz, the smooth nonlinear closed loop is locally asymptotically stable. This is a local result with a model-dependent neighborhood. It does not establish that the linear feedback globally minimizes the nonlinear objective.

A $C^2$ cost has a second-order Taylor model. Its linear term vanishes at an unconstrained stationary minimum, but the Hessian may be singular or zero: $\ell(x)=x^4$ has no nonzero quadratic leading term. Along a general nominal trajectory, retain cost gradients and state-input cross derivatives rather than assuming each stage is at a minimum.

Along a dynamically feasible moving reference, time-varying LQR propagates a value approximation backward from the terminal cost. Solving independent equilibrium Riccati equations at each instant is a different design. The finite-horizon recursion, nonlinear rollout, input constraints, and stability argument must be checked separately. See the [reviewed optimal-control chapter](../The_Geometry_of_Motion/quarto/ch05_optimal_control.qmd).

#### Gain Scheduling Requires Its Own Check

Interpolating locally stabilizing gains does not automatically stabilize the scheduled nonlinear system. For a scheduled Lyapunov metric $P(\rho)$, its derivative contains $\sum_i P_{\rho_i}\dot\rho_i$ as well as the closed-loop Jacobian terms. A common Lyapunov function, appropriate scheduling-rate bounds, or a direct trajectory analysis can supply a certificate. Frozen-point eigenvalues alone do not.

### Lyapunov Stability Analysis

#### Lyapunov's Indirect Method

One of the most powerful tools for analyzing nonlinear stability is **Lyapunov's indirect method**:

::: {.callout-tip}
### Theorem: Lyapunov's Indirect Method

For $f$ continuously differentiable on a neighborhood, consider $\dot{x} = f(x)$ with equilibrium $x_e$ (i.e., $f(x_e) = 0$). Let $A = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_e)$ be the Jacobian at equilibrium.

1. If all eigenvalues of $A$ have strictly negative real parts (Re$(\lambda_i) < 0$), then $x_e$ is **locally asymptotically stable**
2. If any eigenvalue of $A$ has strictly positive real part (Re$(\lambda_j) > 0$), then $x_e$ is **unstable**
3. If all eigenvalues have non-positive real parts with some on imaginary axis, stability is **inconclusive** (higher-order analysis required)
:::

#### Why This Works

For the stable case, write the displacement dynamics as $\dot z=Az+r(z)$, with $r(z)=o(\|z\|)$. If $A$ is Hurwitz, choose $Q\succ0$ and solve $A^\top P+PA=-Q$ for $P\succ0$. Then $V=z^\top Pz$ satisfies

$$
\dot V=-z^\top Qz+2z^\top P r(z).
$$

For a sufficiently small neighborhood, the remainder obeys
$2\|P\|\|r(z)\|\leq\tfrac12\lambda_{\min}(Q)\|z\|$.
Consequently $\dot V\leq-\tfrac12\lambda_{\min}(Q)\|z\|^2$ there. A sufficiently small invariant sublevel set supplies the local stability domain. The proof uses a spectral margin and a bound on the nonlinear remainder; exact differentiation alone is not the certificate.

::: {.callout-note}
### The Pendulum Example Revisited

Recall the pendulum at $x_e = [0,0]^T$ has:

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -g/\ell & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \lambda = \pm i\sqrt{g/\ell}
$$

The eigenvalues are pure imaginary (on the borderline), so Lyapunov's indirect method is **inconclusive**. Indeed, the pendulum equilibrium is:

- Stable (nearby trajectories stay nearby)
- But not asymptotically stable (they don't converge to equilibrium)
- Neutrally stable—consistent with conservative mechanical system

For the inverted pendulum at $x_e = [\pi, 0]^T$, one eigenvalue would be positive, confirming instability.
:::

#### Design and Validation

The pendulum's conserved energy, rather than its imaginary eigenvalues alone, establishes the downward equilibrium's local stability. The inverted equilibrium has a positive eigenvalue and is unstable under the indirect method's hypotheses.

For a controller, first check the feasible equilibrium or reference and the controllable directions. Then design for the stated cost, derive a closed-loop neighborhood bound and compare its predicted outputs against nonlinear rollouts. Gain scheduling and actuator saturation require their own checks. A small region in a chosen norm does not guarantee good performance if an output is highly sensitive or the control margin is small.

Large excursions, contact transitions and changing shaft states can motivate nonlinear control analysis, but their presence alone does not prove that a particular linear controller will fail. The relevant question is whether the proposed controller meets the declared task tolerances over the required domain.

## Residuals, Reference Motion, and Nonlinearity

### An Interaction Requires Four Comparable Trajectories

Fix an initial state, model, time interval, and nominal input $\bar u$. Let $x_{00}$ use $\bar u$, $x_{10}$ use $\bar u+\epsilon v_1$, $x_{01}$ use $\bar u+\epsilon v_2$, and $x_{11}$ use $\bar u+\epsilon(v_1+v_2)$. In a common state coordinate chart, define

$$
r(t_1)=x_{11}(t_1)-x_{10}(t_1)-x_{01}(t_1)+x_{00}(t_1).
$$ {#eq-thesis-residual-def}

The fourth term is the **evolved nominal trajectory**, not the initial state. With zero nominal input it is the evolved zero-input trajectory. For the scalar linear system $\dot x=ax+u$, constant $u$, and duration $T$, the endpoint is $e^{aT}x_0+u(e^{aT}-1)/a$ for $a\ne0$. The four-trajectory residual is zero. Replacing its last term by $x_0$ gives $x_0(1-e^{aT})$, a false interaction even in this linear system.

For $\dot x=u^2$ on the Euclidean line and constant perturbations, the same residual is $2\epsilon^2v_1v_2T$. The state space is flat; the input-to-flow map is nonlinear. Ordinary Hessians depend on coordinates and are not intrinsic Riemann curvature tensors. On a manifold, state subtraction requires a declared chart or retraction and a consistent comparison point.

### First Variations and the Mixed Second Variation

For a fixed finite horizon, assume $f(x,u,t)$ is $C^2$ in state and input on a neighborhood containing the relevant trajectories, with sufficient time regularity and bounded input directions. Let

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot\xi_i&=A(t)\xi_i+B(t)v_i,\qquad \xi_i(t_0)=0,\\
A&=f_x(\bar x,\bar u,t),\qquad B=f_u(\bar x,\bar u,t).
\end{aligned}
$$

These are exact first variations along one nominal trajectory. Their sum obeys the same linear equation. Define $\eta_{12}$ as the mixed second variation of the solution with respect to the two input amplitudes. It satisfies

$$
\dot\eta_{12}=A\eta_{12}+S_{12},\qquad \eta_{12}(t_0)=0,
$$

$$
S_{12}=f_{xx}[\xi_1,\xi_2]+f_{xu}[\xi_1,v_2]
+f_{xu}[\xi_2,v_1]+f_{uu}[v_1,v_2].
$$ {#eq-curvature-connection}

Every derivative is evaluated along the same nominal state and input. For a control-affine system, $f_{uu}=0$, but $f_{xu}$ can be nonzero when the input vector fields depend on state. The interaction is

$$
\begin{aligned}
r(t_1)&=\epsilon^2\eta_{12}(t_1)+o(\epsilon^2),\\
\eta_{12}(t_1)&=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\Phi(t_1,t)S_{12}(t)\,dt.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-residual-scaling}

There is no factor of $1/2$ on this mixed interaction: the two symmetric mixed terms in the Taylor expansion cancel that factor. A single trajectory's second-order Taylor error is a different quantity.

### Transport Is Part of the Bound

For a chosen consistent norm and fixed interval,

$$
\|r(t_1)\|\leq\epsilon^2\int_{t_0}^{t_1}
\|\Phi(t_1,t)\|\,\|S_{12}(t)\|\,dt+o(\epsilon^2).
$$ {#eq-thesis-residual-bound}

The Jacobian matters through $\Phi$ and the first variations inside $S_{12}$. For $\dot x=ax+u^2$, constant directions about $\bar u=0$ give $r=2\epsilon^2v_1v_2(e^{aT}-1)/a$. A constant Hessian source can therefore be amplified exponentially. A bound proportional to $T$ is valid only when its coefficient controls this transport and the other terms over the entire stated interval; it is not a universal linear growth law.

### What a Small Residual Does Not Establish

A small interaction residual does not bound every prediction error. For instance, two input directions may have no mutual interaction while each has its own nonlinear self-effect. A zero denominator also makes $\|r\|/\|\delta x\|$ unusable. Choose physical scales or a metric, a reference magnitude bounded away from zero, and a task tolerance:

$$
\frac{\|r\|_W}{s_{\mathrm{reference}}}\ll1,\qquad s_{\mathrm{reference}}>0.
$$ {#eq-validity-criterion}

This is an interaction diagnostic, not a stability or optimality certificate. Separately check finite-model prediction errors, disturbances, discretization error, and active contact modes. A computation should demonstrate convergence under tighter integration tolerances before calling its residual physical.

## Part II: Integral Superposition and Transport {.unnumbered}

## Fundamentals of Integral Accumulation

### Integration Preserves Linearity

If $g_1,g_2$ are integrable vector-valued functions in one coordinate representation and $a,b$ are fixed scalars, then $\int(ag_1+bg_2)=a\int g_1+b\int g_2$. No dynamic linearity assumption is needed for this algebraic property. The substantive question is whether the integrands being added describe the same experiment.

For first variations along one common reference,

$$
\dot\eta=A(t)\eta+B(t)v(t),\qquad \eta(t_0)=\eta_0.
$$ {#eq-variational-repeat}

The coefficients are fixed by the reference. The derivative direction $v$ may vary over time. Superposition holds between solutions of this linear variational system when initial variations and input directions are combined consistently.

### The Integration Theorem

Direct integration gives the exact identity

$$
\eta(T)-\eta(t_0)
=\int_{t_0}^{T}\bigl(A(t)\eta(t)+B(t)v(t)\bigr)\,dt.
$$ {#eq-integrated-variation}

The first term includes the unknown evolving variation; omitting it is generally incorrect. Introduce the state-transition matrix $\Phi(t,s)$ by $\partial_t\Phi(t,s)=A(t)\Phi(t,s)$ and $\Phi(s,s)=I$. Variation of constants gives

$$
\eta(T)=\Phi(T,t_0)\eta_0+
\int_{t_0}^{T}\Phi(T,t)B(t)v(t)\,dt.
$$ {#eq-endpoint-variation}

To verify the formula, differentiate its right-hand side with respect to $T$. The integral's moving upper limit supplies $B(T)v(T)$, and the derivative of each transition matrix supplies $A(T)$ times the complete expression. Its initial value is $\eta_0$. Uniqueness of the linear initial-value problem then identifies it with $\eta$.

### What Superposes: Variations About One Reference

Let $x_{\epsilon,i}$ use input $\bar u+\epsilon v_i$ from the common initial state, and let $x_{00}$ use $\bar u$. The first variation is

$$
\eta_i(T)=\left.\partial_\epsilon x_{\epsilon,i}(T)\right|_0,
\qquad
x_{\epsilon,i}(T)-x_{00}(T)=\epsilon\eta_i(T)+o(\epsilon).
$$

It is not $x_{\epsilon,i}(T)-x(t_0)$. Subtracting the initial state mixes the nominal displacement with the perturbation response. The sum $\eta_1+\eta_2$ is exactly the derivative for $v_1+v_2$; the finite branched responses retain their nonlinear residual.

When an input or initial condition is uncertain, propagate its joint uncertainty through the common derivative. Summing separate output variances is justified only when the required cross-covariances vanish. Linearity of the variational equation does not establish independence of measured joint torques.

## State Transition Operator

### Solution of the Variational Equation

For zero input variation,

$$
\eta(t)=\Phi(t,s)\eta(s).
$$ {#eq-state-transition-solution}

For finite-dimensional ODEs with continuous coefficients, $\Phi$ is invertible and satisfies $\Phi(t,r)\Phi(r,s)=\Phi(t,s)$ and $\Phi(s,t)=\Phi(t,s)^{-1}$. This is a two-time composition, or cocycle, property. A time-varying system generally depends on both endpoint times, not just their difference.

### Interpretation: Transport Then Accumulate

An input direction applied near time $t$ changes the rate through $B(t)$. The resulting state variation then evolves through $\Phi(T,t)$. A small instantaneous gain can therefore be followed by strong amplification; a large acceleration increment can be followed by cancellation in the selected endpoint output.

Transition matrices at different times need not commute. Take nondimensional matrices

$$
A_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad A_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
$$

on two consecutive unit-duration intervals. Their ordered transition is

$$
e^{A_2}e^{A_1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},
$$

whereas reversing their order gives $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$. Neither equals $e^{A_1+A_2}$. Replacing $\Phi$ by an exponential of an integrated Jacobian needs additional commutation conditions.

### Time-Invariant Special Case

For constant $A$,

$$
\Phi(t,s)=e^{A(t-s)}.
$$ {#eq-matrix-exponential}

The LTI solution is

$$
x(T)=e^{A(T-t_0)}x_0+\int_{t_0}^{T}e^{A(T-t)}Bu(t)\,dt.
$$ {#eq-lti-solution}

This is the complete motion for the linear plant. The same formula with time-varying reference coefficients gives the derivative response for a nonlinear plant; the identical notation does not make the latter a complete nonlinear solution.

## Variational Dynamics and Sensitivity Analysis

### Sensitivity to Initial Conditions

Holding the prescribed input history fixed, define

$$
S_x(t)=D_{x_0}x(t;x_0,\bar u).
$$ {#eq-sensitivity-ic}

Then

$$
S_x(t)=\Phi(t,t_0),
$$ {#eq-sensitivity-phi}

$$
\dot S_x=A(t)S_x,\qquad S_x(t_0)=I.
$$ {#eq-sensitivity-evolution}

For a differentiable output $y=h(x(T))$, its initial-state derivative is $Dh(\bar x(T))\Phi(T,t_0)$. This task map is essential when the state contains angles, velocities and shaft coordinates while the question concerns clubface orientation or impact position.

### An Input Kernel Is a Density

At fixed terminal time and initial state, write

$$
K(T,t)=\Phi(T,t)B(t).
$$ {#eq-sensitivity-input}

The kernel is a **sensitivity density**, to be integrated against an input perturbation and time. If input has torque units, its entries have corresponding state-per-torque-per-time units. It is not generally the derivative of the endpoint with respect to changing a finite torque value at one isolated instant.

For bounded measurable input histories, changing the input at a single time leaves its equivalence class almost everywhere unchanged and does not change the integral solution. A short rectangular pulse of height $\epsilon a$ on $[\tau,\tau+h]$ instead produces the first-order endpoint change $\epsilon\int_\tau^{\tau+h}K(T,t)a\,dt$. For continuous $K$ this approaches $\epsilon h K(T,\tau)a$ as $h$ tends to zero.

For the nondimensional system $\dot x=-x+u$, $x(0)=0$, the exact pulse response is

$$
\Delta x(T)=\epsilon a\,e^{-(T-\tau)}(e^h-1).
$$

At $T=1$, $\tau=0.3$, $\epsilon a=0.2$ and $h=10^{-4}$, it is about $9.9322\times10^{-6}$, not the height-only value $0.2e^{-0.7}$. A Dirac impulse has a specified area and different units; finite impulsive interventions can leave the small-perturbation regime and need their own dynamic interpretation.

### The Endpoint Derivative Is an Operator

Let $\mathcal E(u)=x(T;x_0,u)$ for a fixed interval and initial state. Under uniform smoothness and neighborhood bounds that make this solution map Fréchet differentiable for bounded input histories, its derivative acts on a whole function:

$$
D\mathcal E(\bar u)[v]
=\int_{t_0}^{T}\Phi(T,t)B(t)v(t)\,dt.
$$ {#eq-integrated-sensitivity}

Writing only $\int\Phi B\,dt$ omits the argument. That matrix is the response to a **constant** input-offset parameter, not the entire functional derivative.

In the scalar example at $T=1$, $v(t)=1$ gives $1-e^{-1}\approx0.6321$, while $v(t)=t$ gives $e^{-1}\approx0.3679$. Timing changes the endpoint effect even though both directions use the same kernel. This is a precise reason that the sequence of torque and posture changes matters in the swing.

## Adjoint (Costate) Dynamics

### Backward Sensitivity

For fixed $t_0,T,x_0$, consider

$$
J(u)=\phi(x(T))+\int_{t_0}^{T}L(x(t),u(t),t)\,dt.
$$ {#eq-cost-functional}

Here $L$ is the chosen running cost, not necessarily a mechanical Lagrangian. Use column gradients. Along the prescribed nominal history define an adjoint $\lambda$ so that

$$
\begin{aligned}
C(t,x)&=\phi(X(T))+\int_t^T L(X(s),\bar u(s),s)\,ds,\\
\lambda(t)&=\left.\nabla_x C(t,x)\right|_{x=\bar x(t)}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-costate-def}

Here $X(s)=x(s;t,x,\bar u)$ starts from state $x$ at time $t$. This is the derivative of the future cost when the **future input history is held fixed**. It is not automatically the gradient of the optimally minimized value function.

### Adjoint Evolution Equation

The adjoint solves

$$
\dot\lambda=-A^\top\lambda-L_x,\qquad
$$ {#eq-adjoint-evolution}

$$
\lambda(T)=\phi_x(\bar x(T)).
$$ {#eq-adjoint-terminal}

The first cost variation is

$$
\delta J=\phi_x^\top\eta(T)+
\int_{t_0}^T(L_x^\top\eta+L_u^\top v)\,dt.
$$

Using the forward and backward equations,
$\frac{d}{dt}(\lambda^\top\eta)=-L_x^\top\eta+\lambda^\top Bv$.
Integrating this identity cancels the state-variation terms and yields

$$
DJ(\bar u)[v]=\int_{t_0}^{T}
\bigl(L_u+B^\top\lambda\bigr)^\top v\,dt.
$$ {#eq-optimality-condition}

The quantity $L_u+B^\top\lambda$ is a gradient density for the specified pairing. If the initial state varies, add $\lambda(t_0)^\top\eta_0$. Different inner products on the space of input functions represent the same derivative by different gradients.

For an interior unconstrained stationary input, this density vanishes almost everywhere. With bounds or other constraints, admissible directions are restricted and the appropriate variational inequality or optimal-control conditions replace unrestricted stationarity. Endpoint constraints and variable terminal time also alter boundary conditions.

### The Policy Determines the Sensitivity

If a controller recomputes $u=\kappa(x,t)$ after a state perturbation, the closed-loop state derivative is $A+B\kappa_x$. The running cost becomes $L(x,\kappa(x,t),t)$ and its state gradient includes $\kappa_x^\top L_u$. For $\dot x=x+u$ with $u=-2x$, the closed-loop perturbation decays as $e^{-t}$; freezing the nominal input history instead gives the open-loop sensitivity $e^t$. Both are valid answers to different experiments.

For a golfer, a prescribed torque replay, a model of feedback and a reoptimized motion likewise define different comparisons. An adjoint cannot decide which one represents the player's response.

### A Reproducible Gradient Check

Use the nondimensional system $\dot x=x^2+u$, $x(0)=0.2$, $T=0.3$, nominal $u=0.4$, $\phi=x^2/2$ and $L=(x^2+0.1u^2)/2$. Then $\dot\lambda=-2x\lambda-x$, $\lambda(T)=x(T)$, and the gradient density is $\lambda+0.1u$. For direction $v(t)=1+t$, compare its integral against
$[J(\bar u+\epsilon v)-J(\bar u-\epsilon v)]/(2\epsilon)$ from two independent nonlinear integrations. The supplied regression checks agreement as well as solver accuracy. This verifies the derivative computation for this example; it does not validate a golf model.

### Task and Event Interpretation

An endpoint state sensitivity becomes a clubhead sensitivity only after the appropriate kinematic output derivative is applied. At first contact, the event time usually varies too. For a transversal event $c(x,t)=0$, the time correction has denominator $c_x f+c_t$; a small or zero denominator signals grazing and possible loss of differentiability. Include the event-time derivative, and any impact/reset derivative, before interpreting a pre-impact fixed-time kernel as a ball-strike prediction.

The adjoint weights mechanical effects by a declared objective, while the forward model transports them through changing posture and shaft state. Neither produces a unique allocation of observed performance to muscles, segments or coaching intentions. That inference requires a separately defined intervention and evidence.

## Physical Interpretations: Impulse and Work

## Force-Momentum: Impulse Integral

### Newton's Second Law

For a mechanical Lagrangian $L_m=T-V$ with $p=\partial L_m/\partial\dot q=M(q)\dot q$, the Euler–Lagrange momentum equation can be written:

$$
\frac{dp}{dt} = f(q, \dot{q}) + u
$$ {#eq-newton}

Here $u$ is the chosen generalized applied load and $f=\partial L_m/\partial q+Q_{\mathrm{other}}$. The derivative $\partial L_m/\partial q$ includes configuration-dependent kinetic terms as well as potential forces. Canonical generalized momentum need not equal a Cartesian momentum component. For Cartesian translation with constant mass, the equation reduces to Newton's law with all other external forces included in $f$.

### Impulse Definition

The **impulse** delivered by a force $u$ over $[t_0, t_1]$ is:

$$
J = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} u(\tau) \, d\tau
$$ {#eq-impulse}

From Newton's second law:

$$
\int_{t_0}^{t_1} \frac{dp}{dt} dt = p(t_1) - p(t_0) = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} [f + u] dt
$$ {#eq-impulse-momentum}

If the system starts at rest ($\dot{q}(t_0) = 0$) and the integral of every retained term in $f$ is demonstrably negligible on the stated interval, then approximately:

$$
p(t_1) \approx \int_{t_0}^{t_1} u(\tau) d\tau = J
$$ {#eq-impulse-approx}

The integral of the complete right-hand side equals the canonical momentum change. The impulse of the selected input alone equals that change only when all remaining integrated terms vanish; in Cartesian coordinates the total external impulse equals the change in linear momentum.

### Superposition of Impulses

If two forces $u_1$ and $u_2$ are applied:

$$
\begin{aligned}
J_{12}&=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}[u_1(\tau)+u_2(\tau)]\,d\tau\\
&=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}u_1(\tau)\,d\tau+
\int_{t_0}^{t_1}u_2(\tau)\,d\tau=J_1+J_2.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-impulse-superposition}

This is **exact**—impulses superpose because integration is linear. The resulting momentum change is:

$$
p(t_1) = p(t_0) + J_1 + J_2 + \int_{t_0}^{t_1}f(q(t),\dot q(t))\,dt
$$ {#eq-momentum-superposition}

This is exact bookkeeping on the combined trajectory. The remaining integral is not generally higher order or small; gravity can contribute at first order in elapsed time. If force laws or feedback depend on the state, their actual histories also change across separate counterfactual runs.

::: {.callout-note}
## Interpretation

The complete momentum balance adds retained load terms in one coordinate representation along the actual motion. Its individual input integrals are signed accounting terms, not independent forward-trajectory predictions.
:::

## Power-Energy: Work Integral

### Power and Work

For a mechanical system, **power** delivered by a force is:

$$
P(t) = u(t)^T \dot{q}(t)
$$ {#eq-power}

The **work** done over $[t_0, t_1]$ is:

$$
W = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} P(\tau) d\tau = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} u(\tau)^T \dot{q}(\tau) d\tau
$$ {#eq-work}

For generalized load $u$ paired with $\dot q$, this is the work of that load. The kinetic-energy balance must include the work $W_{\mathrm{other}}$ of all other forces, including gravity when it is not absorbed into potential energy:

$$
W+W_{\mathrm{other}}=E_k(t_1)-E_k(t_0)
$$ {#eq-work-energy}

Here $E_k=\tfrac12\dot q^TM\dot q$. For a time-independent conservative potential and only dissipative loads $-d$ besides $u$, the mechanical-energy balance is $\Delta(E_k+V)=\int(u-d)^T\dot q\,dt$. Ideal stationary constraint reactions do no work; moving supports can. These assumptions must be stated before equating actuator work with an energy change.

### Superposition of Work

If two forces $u_1$ and $u_2$ are applied:

$$
\begin{aligned}
W_{12}&=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}[u_1+u_2]^\top\dot q\,d\tau\\
&=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}u_1^\top\dot q\,d\tau+
\int_{t_0}^{t_1}u_2^\top\dot q\,d\tau=W_1+W_2.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-work-superposition}

Again, **exact** additivity due to integral linearity.

The velocity history is the same combined-motion history in both work terms. For a unit mass initially at rest, two constant unit forces over a unit interval produce velocity $2t$, final kinetic energy 2 and work 1 from each force. Running either force alone gives velocity $t$ and work $1/2$. The separate-run works sum to 1, not 2. This interaction occurs even with linear force-to-velocity dynamics because power multiplies force by velocity.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Variation vs. Causation

The force-work terms add along the same combined trajectory, providing a valid signed energy budget when all terms are included. Those terms are not the works obtained by running each input alone, and normalized work fractions do not uniquely identify physiological causation or efficiency. Negative work and an initial energy store can also make naive percentage interpretations misleading.

Work accounting and first-variation transport are distinct linear operations. Neither automatically assigns a unique fraction of an observed outcome to a physical cause.
:::

## General Principle: Integral Accumulation

Both impulse and work illustrate a general principle:

::: {.callout-important}
## Integral Accumulation Principle

**Along a fixed trajectory** $x(t)$, for any quantity defined as an integral of a linear function of inputs:

$$
\Psi = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} g(x(t), u(t), t) \, dt
$$

where $g$ is linear in $u$ with $x(t)$ held fixed, the contributions from different inputs superpose exactly:

$$
\Psi(u_1 + u_2) = \Psi(u_1) + \Psi(u_2)
$$

**Important caveat:** This integral identity holds for any such input histories evaluated along the same fixed trajectory $x(t)$; the histories need not be infinitesimal. If $x(t)$ itself depends nonlinearly on $u$ (as it generally does in closed-loop or trajectory optimization settings), then the principle does not hold globally — changing $u$ changes the trajectory, and the two contributions cannot be evaluated independently.
:::

Impulse and work are special cases where $g = u$ and $g = u^T \dot{q}$ respectively. The linearity of integration ensures exact additivity of these quantities, even as the underlying dynamics remain nonlinear.

\newpage

## Finite-Horizon Residuals and Error Quantification

### Keep the Baseline and the Perturbation Definition Fixed

The four-trajectory interaction in @eq-thesis-residual-def can also be written using finite deviations $\Delta x_{ij}=x_{ij}-x_{00}$:

$$
r(t_1)=x_{11}(t_1)-x_{10}(t_1)-x_{01}(t_1)+x_{00}(t_1).
$$ {#eq-residual-global}

$$
r=\Delta x_{11}-\Delta x_{10}-\Delta x_{01}.
$$ {#eq-residual-variation}

These finite deviations differ from the first variations $\xi_i$, whose equation is linear and whose interaction is exactly zero. The notation must not quietly turn one into the other.

For a smooth solution map on a fixed interval,

$$
\|r\|=O(\epsilon^2).
$$ {#eq-residual-order}

If $\|\Phi(t_1,t)\|\,\|S_{12}(t)\|\leq C_T$ throughout an interval of duration $T$, then

$$
\|r\|\leq\epsilon^2 C_T T+o(\epsilon^2).
$$ {#eq-residual-bound-time}

$C_T$ can grow rapidly with the horizon. Quadratic order does not mean exact quadrupling at arbitrary amplitudes: the mixed coefficient can vanish, higher orders can matter, and contacts can destroy smooth dependence. Convergence in perturbation amplitude should be tested at a fixed horizon.

### Interaction and Single-Trajectory Approximation Error

The relevant Hessians are

$$
H_x=f_{xx},\qquad H_u=f_{uu},\qquad H_{xu}=f_{xu}.
$$ {#eq-hessians}

The mixed interaction uses $S_{12}$ from @eq-curvature-connection:

$$
r(t_1)=\epsilon^2\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\Phi(t_1,t)S_{12}(t)\,dt+o(\epsilon^2).
$$ {#eq-residual-hessian}

By comparison, a single-input expansion $x_\epsilon=\bar x+\epsilon\xi+\tfrac12\epsilon^2\eta+o(\epsilon^2)$ has a self-variation source $f_{xx}[\xi,\xi]+2f_{xu}[\xi,v]+f_{uu}[v,v]$. Both calculations need transport. Neither identifies intrinsic manifold curvature from a measured residual.

### A Task-Based Interpretation for the Swing

Specify whether comparisons use the same elapsed time or an event such as first ball contact. A perturbed trajectory may reach that event at a different time, so a contact-event endpoint map must include event-time sensitivity; smooth-flow expressions alone do not provide it. A changed contact mode requires a hybrid analysis.

In a common coordinate chart, compare residuals using declared scales:

$$
\chi=\|r\|_W/s_{\mathrm{reference}},\qquad s_{\mathrm{reference}}>0.
$$ {#eq-validity-quantitative}

If the chosen perturbation response scale is proportional to $\epsilon$, a bounded mixed response gives a diagnostic of order

$$
\chi=O(\epsilon C_T T).
$$ {#eq-validity-simplified}

For a prescribed tolerance $\chi_{\max}$, a leading-order estimate is

$$
\epsilon C_T T\lesssim\chi_{\max},
$$ {#eq-validity-epsilon}

with scales absorbed into $C_T$. It is meaningful only where the derivative bounds and remainder estimates hold. There is no universal threshold such as 0.1 at which a nonlinear controller becomes necessary.

Applied to a swing model, this procedure can quantify how two chosen input interventions interact in club position, face orientation, or speed. It does not recover a unique causal allocation of observed performance to muscles. Geometry, state-dependent leverage, activation, shaft storage, feedback, and impact timing can all alter the endpoint map. Compare those mechanisms through explicit model variants and measured uncertainties.
